1.札幌市: Written "satsuhoro" in 17th-century records and "札縨" by the late Edo period; in Meiji the second character became 幌, giving 札幌. The name is generally traced to Ainu.

4.仙台市: The usual account: the Kokubun clan called their castle Sendai "千代" (a thousand Buddha images stood there) and Date Masamune rewrote it as 仙臺 after a Tang poem. Ainu origins are also proposed.

6.山形市: From "Yamakata" — the place at the foot of the Zaō range.

7.郡山市: The district office (gunga) of the ancient ritsuryō state stood here.

9.宇都宮市: Usually traced to Utsunomiya Daimyōjin, another name of Futarasan Shrine, the first shrine of Shimotsuke; other explanations exist.

10.高崎市: Once called Wada. Legend says Ii Naomasa wanted "Matsugasaki", but the priest Hakuan suggested Takasaki, "lofty success".
10.前橋市: Originally Mayabashi: a bridge over the Kuruma River was called the bridge of the post station (umaya), and the name stuck. It became Maebashi between 1648 and 1652, under the lord Sakai Tadakiyo.

11.川越市: Directly from the Kawagoe clan of the Heian period; "kawa-goe" (across the river) or "kawa-koe" (river-fertilised) are both proposed.
11.川口市: "Kogawaguchi" appears in the late-Kamakura memoir Towazugatari — the meeting of the Shiba and Iruma (now Ara) rivers.
11.所沢市: Said to mean a marsh thick with tokoro (a wild yam), once written 野老澤.
11.越谷市: "Koshi" (foot of the hills) + "ya" (low wetland): the lowland below the Ōmiya terrace. The ヶ was dropped in 1954 to tell the new town from old Koshigaya.

12.船橋市: Legend says Yamato Takeru crossed the Ebi River on a bridge of boats — a "funabashi".
12.松戸市: Theories include "uma-sato" (horse village, near the Koganemaki pastures) and "matsu-sato", a place of waiting — for Yamato Takeru's men or the ferry.

13.新宿区: From Naitō-Shinjuku, a new post town opened on the Kōshū road in 1698 on land of the Naitō lords of Takatō.
13.江東区: "East of the river" — east of the Sumida; chosen over Tatsumi, Higashi and Eitai.
13.大田区: One character each from Ōmori and Kamata, the two wards merged in 1947.
13.杉並区: From the row of cedars planted along the Ōme road by the lord of Narimune and Tabata villages in the early Edo period.
13.板橋区: From the "plank bridge" carrying the old Nakasendō over the Shakujii River.
13.練馬区: Several theories: Nerima Castle; a "neriba" where red loam was kneaded; or the Nara-period post station Norinuma.
13.足立区: From Adachi district of Musashi, set up after the Taika reforms.
13.葛飾区: Katsushika was the name of a wide district of Shimōsa, already in the Man'yōshū; this area itself was called Kasai until early modern times.
13.江戸川区: From the Edo River on its eastern edge; "Matsue-ku", after the planned ward office, was considered first.
13.八王子市: From the Hachiōji shrine and Hachiōji Castle named after it.
13.町田市: Theories: "machi" as a block of paddy; a busy market (machi = ichi); or "matsurida", fields kept for the market god.

14.横浜市: A beach that runs long and sideways seen from the sea — "yoko-hama".

15.新潟市: Recorded by 1520 but of uncertain origin: a new lagoon (kata) at the Shinano River mouth, or "Niikata", a new settlement.

16.富山市: First recorded as Toyama-gō, "outer mountain", east of Mount Kureha at the edge of Imizu district; later written 富山.

17.金沢市: From the legend of Imohori Tōgorō, who washed gold dust from a spring; the town was also called Oyama, and the Maeda used both names.

19.甲府市: Takeda Nobutora named it in 1519 when he moved his seat to Tsutsujigasaki: the "capital of Kai".

20.長野市: First seen in a 1570 letter of Takeda Shingen: "long, gently sloping land" on the Susobana River fan.

21.岐阜市: Oda Nobunaga renamed the castle town of Inokuchi "Gifu" after taking Mino.

22.浜松市: Wooden tags from the Iba site read "Hamatsu" (tsu = harbour); it became Hamamatsu between the late Heian and Kamakura periods.
22.静岡市: Long called Fuchū. In the early Meiji years the new government ordered the confusing name changed; the domain proposed Shizu, Shizuki and Shizuoka, and Shizuoka was chosen. "Shizu" is said to come from Mount Shizuhata.

23.一宮市: Home of Masumida Shrine, the first shrine (ichinomiya) of Owari.

26.京都市: "Kyōto" was simply a word for "capital"; centuries as the seat of the court made it this city's name.

27.堺市: It sat on the border (sakai) of Settsu and Izumi provinces.
27.吹田市: Said to begin with the Sukita clan crossing the Yodo River around the 5th century; other theories exist.
27.高槻市: Once "Takatsuki" with the character for moon; it changed to the zelkova tree (槻) after a camp was set by a great tree in the Sengoku period.

28.神戸市: The houses around today's Sannomiya were kanbe, households supporting Ikuta Shrine; "kanbe" became "kōbe".
28.姫路市: From Himeji Hill, the old name of the castle hill, already in the Harima Fudoki; a link to silkworms (himeko) is also suggested.

29.奈良市: Most likely from the flat, "levelled" (nara-su) land; also written 那羅, 寧楽 and 平城.

30.和歌山市: Hideyoshi named it Wakayama after the famous scenic bay of Waka-no-ura.

33.倉敷市: From kurashikichi, the medieval depots where tax rice was gathered before shipping to the lords.

34.広島市: The name came with Mōri Terumoto's castle on the Ōta delta: either the broad island of the delta, or "Hiro" from the Mōri ancestor Ōe no Hiromoto plus "shima" from a local lord.
34.福山市: The castle hill was "Bat Mountain"; the bat character sounds like fuku (fortune), so the first lord Mizuno Katsunari named it Fukuyama.

37.高松市: From Takatsu-gō in a mid-Heian chronicle; Ikoma Chikamasa renamed the castle area, then "Nohara", Takamatsu in 1588.

39.高知市: The flood-prone castle between rivers was "Kōchiyama" (mountain amid the river), rewritten 高智山 and shortened to Kōchi.

40.北九州市: Already in use before the merger — the Nishitetsu Kitakyūshū line (from 1942) and wartime papers naming the five cities of Moji, Kokura, Tobata, Wakamatsu and Yahata.
40.久留米市: Written 久留目 by the Muromachi period; explanations include the god Kurume and immigrant weavers (kurebe).

18.福井市: Known as Kitanoshō in the Muromachi period, when Shibata Katsuie built his castle town here. Under the third lord, Tadamasa, it became 福居 (Fukui), later written 福井.

36.徳島市: In 1585, when Hachisuka Iemasa built his castle, the area called Inotsu was renamed Tokushima; who chose the name, and why, is not recorded. It later reverted to Inotsu until the fifth lord, Tsunanori, restored Tokushima in 1678.

38.松山市: Named in 1603 after the castle site built by Katō Yoshiaki. Two explanations for the "pine": the castle hill was planted with many pines, or the character came from the Tokugawa-related Matsudaira family (per the Edo-period Yoyō gungō rigenshū).

42.長崎市: Several explanations exist; the city's own account is that the land was a long cape — naga-saki.

47.那覇市: From naha, "fishing ground" — Iha Fuyū's explanation, also given by the city.
